question: Climb into thinner air and watch water boil. Why can't a cup of water stay liquid on Mars, even on a warm afternoon?
answer: The air is too thin to hold it. Water boils when its vapour pushes as hard as the air above, so thinner air means a lower boiling point. Mars's surface pressure, about 6 millibars, sits near the 6.1 below which water cannot be liquid at all: ice turns straight to vapour.
move: Warmth alone does not make a liquid; the pressure has to allow it.
ask: What second condition besides the obvious one decides whether my plan can work?
source: Haberle et al., 2001; US Standard Atmosphere
reference: Haberle, McKay, Schaeffer et al., On the possibility of liquid water on present-day Mars, Journal of Geophysical Research: Planets 106(E10), 2001; U.S. Standard Atmosphere, 1976, NOAA, NASA and US Air Force

notes.text: Sea level: 100 °C, the number everyone learns.
The top of Everest: water boils at about 70 °C.
About 19 km: it boils at 37 °C, body heat. Pilots call it the Armstrong limit.
About 34 km, air as thin as Mars's: liquid only between 0 and 1 °C.
